topic: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
parentTitle: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
title: Recovery, trauma-informed care and stigma
blurb: Use CHIME and the six trauma-informed principles to plan care that builds hope, avoids retraumatisation and challenges stigma.
question: Nadia, 35, has schizophrenia and a history of childhood abuse. She refuses to let a male nurse do her night checks and says, 'There's no point planning anything, people like me don't get better.' How should the nurse respond?

teach.body: Clinical recovery means symptoms going away. Personal recovery means living a satisfying, hopeful and contributing life, with or without ongoing symptoms. Mental health services in the UK aim for personal recovery, defined by the person, not the professional. Plain English: recovery is not 'cured'; it is getting your life back on your own terms.

teach.h: CHIME: the processes of personal recovery
teach.caption: Leamy et al. (2011) systematic review. Useful for care plans: which CHIME area is the person's goal building?
Working definition of trauma-informed practice, OHID, 2 Nov 2022.

teach.body: OHID defines trauma as an event, series of events or set of circumstances experienced by a person as harmful or life threatening. Trauma-informed practice means realising how common trauma is and how it affects people, recognising its signs, and preventing re-traumatisation. On a ward, restraint, seclusion, searches, being watched at night or care from someone who reminds a person of an abuser can all re-traumatise. OHID asks practitioners to look beyond behaviour and ask 'What does this person need?' rather than 'What is wrong with this person?'.
teach.cite: OHID working definition of trauma-informed practice (2022)

teach.caption: Self-stigma grows when people absorb public stereotypes; it erodes hope and help-seeking.

items: Use person-first, respectful language in speech and records.
Share recovery stories and offer peer support workers.
Make reasonable adjustments under the Equality Act 2010 (s20) for disabled people, including those with mental health conditions.

teach.body: The nurse treats Nadia's request as a trauma-informed choice, not 'difficult behaviour': she arranges for a female nurse to do night checks and explains when and how checks will happen (safety, choice, trustworthiness). She responds to Nadia's hopelessness by naming it gently as something many people feel, and offers hope: people with schizophrenia can and do build good lives. Together they set one small goal Nadia chooses, linked to CHIME.

teach.text: Recovery does NOT mean being symptom-free or off medication. And trauma-informed care is not a therapy only specialists deliver: it is a way every nurse works, giving safety, choice and control, and avoiding practices that re-traumatise.

items: Personal recovery = a meaningful life defined by the person, with or without symptoms.
CHIME: Connectedness, Hope, Identity, Meaning, Empowerment.
Trauma-informed principles (OHID 2022): safety, trustworthiness, choice, collaboration, empowerment, cultural consideration.
Stigma acts at self, public and structural levels; challenge it with language, action and hope.

summary: You can now explain personal recovery and use CHIME to shape care plans. You can also apply the six trauma-informed principles to avoid retraumatisation and challenge stigma in everyday practice.

A.q: In the CHIME recovery framework, what does the 'H' stand for?
options: Health and wellbeing
Hope and optimism
Housing and stability
Help-seeking
A.why: CHIME: Connectedness, Hope and optimism, Identity, Meaning in life, Empowerment (Leamy et al., 2011).

whyNot.0: Health is not the H in CHIME.
whyNot.2: Housing matters to recovery but is not the H in CHIME.
whyNot.3: Help-seeking is not one of the five processes.

A.q: Which is one of the six principles in the OHID working definition of trauma-informed practice?
options: Compliance
Containment
Choice
Confrontation
A.why: OHID (2022): safety, trustworthiness, choice, collaboration, empowerment and cultural consideration.

whyNot.0: Compliance runs against empowerment and choice.
whyNot.1: Containment is not one of the six principles.

A.q: What does 'personal recovery' mean in mental health care?
options: A full and permanent absence of symptoms
Discharge from all mental health services
Stopping all psychiatric medication
A meaningful life defined by the person
A.why: Personal recovery is about living a satisfying, hopeful life as defined by the person, with or without ongoing symptoms.

whyNot.0: This describes clinical recovery or cure.
whyNot.1: Discharge is a service outcome, not personal recovery.
whyNot.2: Many people in recovery continue medication.

B.q: A newly admitted woman with a history of sexual assault becomes very distressed when told she will be searched by two staff. Which trauma-informed response is best?
options: Explain, offer choices such as a female searcher, go at her pace
Proceed quickly so the distressing part is over sooner for her
Postpone the search indefinitely to avoid causing any distress
Ask the security team to carry out the search for the ward instead
B.why: Safety, trustworthiness and choice: explain what will happen and why, offer choices where possible (such as gender of staff) and give her control over pace.

whyNot.1: Rushing removes control and can re-traumatise.
whyNot.2: A needed safety search should be adapted, not abandoned.
whyNot.3: Unfamiliar security staff are likely to increase threat and distress.

B.q: A man with bipolar disorder says, 'I'm just a mental case; I'll never hold down a job.' Which type of stigma is he showing?
options: Public stigma
Structural stigma
Self-stigma
Courtesy stigma
B.why: Self-stigma is when a person accepts negative stereotypes about mental illness and applies them to themselves, reducing hope and self-esteem.

whyNot.0: Public stigma is held by others in society.
whyNot.1: Structural stigma lies in policies and systems.
whyNot.3: Courtesy stigma affects people associated with the person, such as family.

B.q: Which entry in a nursing record best reflects recovery-oriented, person-first language?
options: 'The schizophrenic in bed 4 was non-compliant.'
'Patient refused meds again, as usual.'
'Attention-seeking behaviour noted at 14:00.'
'Mr Ali chose not to take his 10:00 dose.'
B.why: Person-first, factual and non-judgemental language respects the person and avoids stigmatising labels.

whyNot.0: Defining someone by a diagnosis and 'non-compliant' is stigmatising.
whyNot.1: 'As usual' is judgemental and not factual.
whyNot.2: 'Attention-seeking' is a pejorative label, not a description.

C.q: Nadia wants to start a college course. The team worries that stress might trigger relapse. Which approach best supports recovery?
options: Advise her to wait until she has been well for 2 years
Plan with her: weigh risks, add support, agree warning signs
Refuse to support the course until her symptoms fully resolve
Let her go ahead and withdraw team support
C.why: Recovery-oriented care supports the person's own goals with shared, positive risk-taking: plan supports and relapse signs together.

whyNot.0: An arbitrary wait undermines hope and her choice.
whyNot.2: Waiting for symptom resolution confuses clinical and personal recovery.
whyNot.3: Support should continue to make her goal achievable.

C.q: After a restraint, a man with a history of childhood violence is shaking and refusing to speak. Which action best fits trauma-informed practice?
options: Leave him in his room until he is ready to apologise
Record the incident and move on to other tasks
Offer a debrief with a trusted staff member when he is ready
Warn him that any further incidents will lead to seclusion
C.why: Restraint can re-traumatise; offering a supported debrief, with a trusted person when he is ready, restores safety, trust and collaboration.

whyNot.0: Demanding an apology is punitive and blaming.
whyNot.1: Recording is necessary but not sufficient; his distress needs a response.
whyNot.3: Threats increase fear and are not therapeutic.

C.q: A colleague says in handover, 'Don't bother with care planning for him, schizophrenics don't get better.' What should the nurse do?
options: Challenge the comment and share evidence of recovery
Agree privately but complete the care plan anyway
Raise it later in a private chat after the shift
Ask the patient whether he minds the comment
C.why: Code 3.4 and 20.2 require challenging discriminatory attitudes; respectfully challenging and offering a recovery perspective protects care and culture.

whyNot.2: Delaying lets the attitude shape care in this handover; challenge it respectfully at the time.
whyNot.3: Responsibility for challenging staff attitudes lies with staff, not the patient.

reteach.title: Hope, choice and safety
reteach.question: What does a trauma-informed, recovery-focused nurse actually do?

blocks.body: Ask what matters to the person and what has happened to them. Offer choices wherever you can. Explain what will happen and keep your word. Hold hope for the person until they can hold it themselves.

blocks.h: Where recovery and trauma-informed care meet

blocks.text: Recovery is not the same as being symptom-free.

explain.body: Connectedness, Hope and optimism, Identity, Meaning in life, Empowerment: the processes of personal recovery.

test.q: A care plan goal is 'Join the allotment group to meet people.' Which CHIME process does it mainly build?
options: Empowerment
Identity
Meaning in life
Connectedness
test.why: Meeting people and belonging to a group builds connectedness, the C in CHIME.

whyNot.0: Empowerment is about control and strengths.
whyNot.1: Identity is about rebuilding a positive sense of self.
whyNot.2: Meaning relates to purpose, though the main aim here is meeting people.

explain.body: Safety, trustworthiness, choice, collaboration, empowerment, cultural consideration (OHID 2022).

options: An event experienced by a person as harmful or life threatening
A diagnosis of post-traumatic stress disorder made by a psychiatrist
Any stressful event or situation lasting longer than 1 month
A physical injury that needed emergency hospital treatment
test.why: OHID: trauma results from an event, series of events or set of circumstances experienced by an individual as harmful or life threatening.

whyNot.1: Trauma is broader than a PTSD diagnosis.
whyNot.2: Duration is not part of the definition.
whyNot.3: Trauma is defined by experience, not physical injury.

explain.body: Restraint, seclusion, searches, observation, loss of control and staff resembling abusers can re-traumatise. Prevent it by explanation, choice and collaboration.

test.q: Which ward practice is most likely to re-traumatise a person with a history of abuse?
options: Explaining the ward routine on admission
Unexplained night checks by unfamiliar staff
Offering a choice of named nurse
Agreeing a plan for how to calm down
test.why: Unexplained intrusions by strangers remove safety and control, echoing past trauma.

explain.body: Self, public and structural stigma. Use person-first, factual language; challenge discrimination (Code 3.4, 20.2); reasonable adjustments (Equality Act s20).

test.q: Which phrase is the most respectful way to describe a person in a care plan?
options: 'A depressive'
'A person living with depression'
'Suffers from depression'
'Depressed patient, non-engaging'
test.why: Person-first language puts the person before the diagnosis and avoids pejorative labels.

whyNot.0: This defines the person by the diagnosis.
whyNot.2: 'Suffers from' frames the person as a victim.
whyNot.3: This combines a label with a judgemental term.
